notes.h: Location and extent of the Greater Dublin Area
notes.b: The Greater Dublin Area (GDA) is the core region of Ireland's east coast, facing Britain and Europe across the Irish Sea. Knowing exactly which counties it includes is the starting point for every question on it.
points: The GDA is Dublin City and County Dublin, plus Counties Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. Louth, including Drogheda, is not part of it, so do not count it.

Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown are the four local authorities (the councils that run local services) of Dublin; the single Co. Dublin county council was split into the last three in 1994.
notes.tip: Name all four counties when you define the region, and do not include Louth.

notes.h: Why the GDA is a core region
notes.b: A core region is one that concentrates people, wealth and services, in contrast to peripheral regions (remote areas with fewer of these). The GDA fits this description in several ways.
points: Its large, dense and growing population is the largest in the State, which gives firms customers and workers.
It holds most of the State's wealth, jobs, multinational investment, government and services, which means firms and workers want to be there.
It has the best infrastructure in the State, including the main port, airport and motorway network, so goods and people move easily.
It attracts in-migrants (people moving in) from the rest of Ireland and from abroad.
Cumulative causation (growth that feeds more growth): growth attracts firms and workers, which attracts further investment and widens the gap with peripheral regions such as the West.
notes.tip: If asked to name a core region and explain why it is core, name the GDA and give reasons such as population, wealth and jobs, infrastructure and in-migration.

notes.b: A sketch map of the region is set as a question, and it is marked on a handful of simple features. Draw these, each clearly labelled.
points: Outline the four counties: Dublin and Wicklow on the coast, Meath to the north (with a short coastline south of the Boyne estuary), Kildare to the west.
Draw the River Liffey from the Wicklow Mountains, through Kildare, to Dublin Bay.
Draw the River Boyne through Trim and Navan, reaching the sea at Drogheda, just outside the GDA.
Mark Dublin city, and the towns of Navan, Naas and Bray.
Show relief (the height and shape of the land): the Wicklow Mountains in the south and the lowland plain of Meath and Kildare, so the map shows both upland and lowland.
notes.tip: A sketch map asks for the outline of the region, one river, one or two urban centres and one relief feature.

notes.b: The GDA has a cool temperate oceanic climate (mild and wet because of the nearby ocean), with prevailing south-westerly winds bringing moist Atlantic air. Because of where the mountains sit, the east is drier than the west.
points: Rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of high ground): the Wicklow Mountains and the uplands further west force moist air to drop its rain on the western slopes, so the east is the driest part of Ireland.
Rainfall in the east is about 750–1,000 mm a year, so it is much drier than the west; Dublin Airport records about 750 mm.
By contrast, the west receives 1,000–1,250 mm a year and some mountains exceed 2,000 mm.
The south-east is the sunniest part of Ireland, which adds to the east's value for crops.
Mean January temperatures in Ireland are about 4–7 °C and mean July temperatures about 14–16 °C, so winters are mild and summers cool.
Being farther from the Atlantic than the west gives a slightly greater temperature range: warmer summers, colder winters and more frost.
Heavier rain and snow fall on the Wicklow uplands than on the lowlands, because rising air cools and drops its moisture.
notes.tip: To explain why the east is drier and sunnier than the west, give the rain shadow and the distance from the Atlantic.

notes.h: Climate: effects on farming and land use
notes.b: Climate decides what the land can be used for. The dry east and the wet uplands are used in different ways.
points: Effect on farming: the dry, relatively sunny lowlands suit tillage (growing crops such as cereals and vegetables) and horticulture (growing vegetables, fruit and flowers).
Effect on land use: heavy upland rain supports conifer forestry and reservoirs, because the rain feeds fast-growing trees and fills water stores.
notes.tip: When the question asks about physical factors for agriculture, link each climate point to its effect on farming.

notes.b: Relief means the height and shape of the land. The GDA has a wide lowland to the north and west and a mountain block to the south, and each is used differently.
points: A low-lying, gently undulating lowland covers most of Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin, part of the Central Lowlands.
The Central Lowlands are underlain by Carboniferous limestone (a sedimentary rock), covered by glacial deposits.

The Wicklow and Dublin Mountains lie to the south, with a core of the Leinster granite batholith (a huge mass of granite that cooled underground), about 400 million years old (Caledonian, the mountain-building episode that made it).
Lugnaquilla, 925 m, in Co. Wicklow, is the highest peak in Leinster, so it is a good example of the region's upland relief.
Kippure, about 757 m, stands on the Dublin–Wicklow border, so the mountains are close enough to the city to be used for recreation.
The Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow, is a quartzite peak (quartzite is a very hard rock) that stands out from the granite.
Effect: the lowland is easy to farm, build on and cross with roads and rail; the uplands suit forestry, water supply and recreation.
notes.tip: Exams ask for physical factors, so state the effect of relief on farming, building and transport, not just the landform.

notes.b: Ice sheets and the sea have both shaped the region. These named landforms are the examples to use.
points: The U-shaped valleys (steep-sided, flat-floored valleys) of Glendalough and Glenmalure were carved by glacial erosion, which is why their sides are steep and their floors flat.
Esker Riada is a long ridge of sand and gravel deposited by glacial meltwater, which is why it is made of loose, rounded material.
Howth Head is joined to the mainland by the Sutton tombolo (a bar of sand or shingle linking an island or headland to the land).
North Bull Island lies in Dublin Bay, so it is an example of a coastal feature there.

notes.b: Soil follows the rock and drainage beneath it. The lowlands have deep, fertile soils, while the granite uplands and bogs have poor ones, so soil sets how land is used.
points: Deep, fertile brown earths (a well-developed soil rich in nutrients) on limestone boulder clay (stony clay left by ice sheets) cover Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin, among the best farmland in Ireland.
Brown earths are well drained, which suits both tillage and grassland.
The Curragh, Co. Kildare, has free-draining sand and gravel from glacial outwash (material washed out from the ice by meltwater), with well-drained grassland used for horse training.
The Bog of Allen, Co. Kildare, is a raised bog (a dome of peat built up from dead plants) of deep peat, which is unsuitable for farming unless drained.
Blanket bog (peat covering the ground like a blanket) on granite at the Sally Gap, Co. Wicklow, is waterlogged and acidic, so it is of little use for farming.
Acidic, leached podzols (grey soils with nutrients washed out of the top layer) cover the granite uplands of Wicklow, poor for farming but suitable for conifers.
Effect on land use: fertile lowland soils support farming; thin, acidic upland soils and bog are used for forestry, recreation and water catchment (land that collects rain for a river or reservoir).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to account for patterns, so give each soil with its location and the land use it leads to.

notes.b: Drainage covers the rivers, canals and reservoirs of the region. In the GDA they matter because a large city needs a reliable water supply.
points: The River Liffey rises in the Wicklow Mountains, flows through Kildare and enters the sea at Dublin Bay, so it links upland to city.
The Poulaphouca dam on the Liffey created the Blessington Lakes reservoir, used for hydro-electricity and for Dublin's drinking water.
The Vartry Reservoir at Roundwood, Co. Wicklow, supplies Dublin with water, so the uplands serve the city.
The River Boyne flows through Trim and Navan, Co. Meath, and reaches the sea near Drogheda, outside the GDA, so its mouth is not in the region.
The smaller Dublin rivers, the Dodder and the Tolka, flow through the city to Dublin Bay, so they drain urban areas.
The Royal and Grand Canals link Dublin to the River Shannon, so they connect the east coast to the interior.
Uisce Éireann (Irish Water) has proposed a pipeline to bring water from the River Shannon to the Dublin region, because demand on local supplies is growing.
Paved surfaces in the city let rain run off quickly into rivers, raising urban flood risk.
notes.tip: Do not give a length for the Liffey or the Boyne.

notes.b: Farming does well in the GDA because physical and human advantages come together. Each factor below can be developed as a separate point in an answer.
points: Climate: the dry, relatively sunny east suits tillage (growing crops) and horticulture (growing vegetables and similar crops).
Relief: flat lowland allows large fields and mechanised farming, which cuts the cost of each crop.
Soils: deep, fertile brown earths in Meath and Kildare give high-quality land for crops and grass.
Market: Dublin, the largest urban area in the State, lies on the farms' doorstep, so produce has a short journey to many buyers.
Transport: Dublin Port and Dublin Airport export farm produce and livestock, so farmers can sell abroad.
Policy and technology: EU and Irish agricultural policy and modern machinery support large, productive farms.
notes.tip: Agriculture questions ask for factors such as climate, relief and markets. This region gives the favourable example when two regions are compared.

notes.b: Farming here is large-scale and commercial, but each county specialises in something different, shaped by its soil, relief and nearness to Dublin.
points: Large, commercial and highly productive farms dominate the lowlands, because the flat, fertile land suits them.
Meath, for example: beef cattle fattening (raising cattle to slaughter weight) and tillage on large farms.
Kildare: bloodstock (breeding of racehorses) and racehorse training, centred on the Curragh racecourse and the Irish National Stud at Tully, Kildare town.
Fingal, for example: horticulture, with field vegetables and glasshouse crops centred on Rush and Lusk.
Wicklow: sheep grazing on the upland pasture of the Wicklow Mountains, because the steep, poor land suits sheep better than crops.
notes.tip: Name the county with each farm type, as in Rush and Lusk for horticulture and the Curragh for bloodstock.

notes.b: The pressure of a huge city next door is the main problem for farmers in the GDA, along with market and policy pressures.
points: Urban sprawl (spread of housing and industry outward from the city) takes farmland for housing and industry.
High land prices, especially near Dublin, push farmers to sell land to developers.
Part-time farming is common near the city, where farm owners depend on jobs off the farm, because farm income alone is not enough.
Horticulture needs seasonal labour, which is costly and sometimes in short supply.
Growers face competition from imported vegetables, which can undercut their prices.
Changes to the rules of the EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP, the EU's farm support scheme) alter farm incomes and force farmers to adapt.
notes.tip: Describe these problems without numbers, since there are no checked figures for house prices or land prices.

notes.b: Forestry uses the land that is too poor to farm. In the GDA that means the Wicklow uplands, though forests cover only a small share of Ireland.
points: Wicklow is among Ireland's most forested counties and is known as the Garden of Ireland, because so much of its upland is wooded.
Conifer plantations, mainly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), grow on poor upland soils unsuited to farming.
Coillte, the State forestry company set up in 1988, has its head office at Newtownmountkennedy, Co. Wicklow.
Wicklow Mountains National Park, set up in 1991, protects the upland landscape and provides recreation, so it serves both conservation and visitors.
Forest recreation areas near Dublin are used by city residents for walking and cycling, because they are close to the city.
Ireland's forest cover is about 11% (2020s), one of the lowest in the EU, so forestry covers a small share of the land.

notes.b: Fishing is only a small part of the region's economy. The main facts are Howth, the quota rules and the shrinking fleet.
points: Fishing is a small part of the region's economy, so the region depends little on it.
Howth, Co. Dublin, is one of Ireland's six State-owned Fishery Harbour Centres (harbours run by the State for the fishing industry).
The other five are Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel and Dunmore East; none is in the GDA.
Dublin Bay prawns and whitefish, for example, are landed at Howth.
EU Common Fisheries Policy quotas (limits on the amount of each fish species that may be caught) limit how much Irish boats can catch.
The 2020 EU–UK Brexit trade agreement reduced Irish fishing quotas.
The fishing fleet has been falling in size, which is partly a result of the quota limits.
notes.tip: Keep fishing brief. The problems to give are EU quotas, the loss of quota after Brexit and the falling fleet.

notes.b: The region's rocks and glacial deposits supply minerals and building materials. Tara Mines at Navan is the largest operation.
points: Tara Mines at Navan, Co. Meath, is an underground zinc and lead mine, opened in 1977 (paused from July 2023, restarted at the end of 2024).
Tara Mines is Europe's largest zinc mine, and is owned by Boliden.
Sand and gravel are quarried from glacial deposits for construction, because the ice sheets left large amounts of them.
Granite is quarried at Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow.
Bord na Móna has ended peat harvesting in the Bog of Allen, Co. Kildare, where peat was once cut for fuel.
notes.tip: Say that Bord na Móna has ended peat harvesting, and give no date.

notes.b: A big population and many businesses make the GDA Ireland's largest energy market. Its power comes from several sources.
points: The GDA is Ireland's largest energy market, because it has the most people and businesses.
Poolbeg, Ringsend, has gas-fired power generation on Dublin Bay.
The Dublin Waste-to-Energy incinerator, operating since 2017, generates electricity by burning waste.
Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow, is an ESB pumped-storage station built in 1974: water is pumped uphill at night and released to generate power at peak demand.
Arklow Bank Wind Park off Co. Wicklow is Ireland's first offshore wind farm, so it uses wind over the sea rather than land.
Data centres (buildings full of computer servers) used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), most of them in the Dublin region.
The East–West Interconnector carries electricity by cable to Wales from near Rush, Co. Dublin.
notes.tip: Do not describe Poolbeg's tall chimneys as working, because they belong to the old ESB oil-fired station, which is closed.

notes.b: The GDA is where most Irish manufacturing is found, but the location of factories within it has shifted outward over time.
points: The GDA is Ireland's largest manufacturing region, which is why its factory locations matter for exams.
Older industries near Dublin Port and in the inner city, such as brewing, food and port-related industry, declined as older plants closed.
Newer high-tech and pharmaceutical plants are in suburban business parks and towns near the M50 (the orbital motorway around Dublin) and motorways.
Examples of these locations are Grange Castle near Clondalkin, Leixlip and Blanchardstown.
Production has moved from the inner city to edge-of-city sites because they offer space and road access.

notes.h: Case study: Intel, Pfizer and Guinness
notes.b: Three firms show the pattern: two modern plants on the edge of the city and one old brewery still working in the inner city.
points: Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare, opened in 1989 and is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Intel's high-tech plant lies near the M4, which links it to Dublin Airport and Dublin Port, so products can be exported quickly.
Pfizer's biopharmaceutical (medicine-making) plant is at Grange Castle Business Park, Clondalkin.
Guinness's St James's Gate Brewery was founded in 1759 on a 9,000-year lease.
Guinness at St James's Gate shows, for example, that an older inner-city industry can survive beside newer high-tech plants.
notes.tip: Higher Level answers on secondary activity expect Intel and pharmaceutical examples, with each factor developed in detail. Do not give job numbers for Intel.

notes.b: A market is a group of customers. The GDA has a large one on its doorstep and easy routes to larger ones abroad.
points: The GDA has about 2.1 million people, the largest concentration of consumers in the State.
Dublin Port and Dublin Airport give access to the EU single market (the EU area where goods move without trade barriers).
Ferries from Dublin Port to Holyhead, Wales, give access to the British market, which is the nearest large foreign market.
Dublin Airport allows high-value products to be shipped quickly by air to customers across Europe and beyond.
Together, the port and airport link the region to foreign markets for exports.
notes.tip: Two factors are asked for, each developed in several points, so use the specific port, airport and ferry facts.

notes.b: Modern plants need skilled workers. The GDA has the largest and best-educated pool of labour in the State.
points: The GDA has a large, young, educated workforce, so firms can fill technical jobs.
Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin, Dublin City University, Technological University Dublin and Maynooth University (Co. Kildare) produce graduates for technical and research jobs.
Immigrant workers add skills and languages to the workforce, which helps firms that sell abroad.
Commuters from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow widen the pool of workers, so firms can recruit from beyond the city.
A concentration of skilled workers attracts firms that need specialist staff, so labour reinforces the other factors.

notes.b: Infrastructure means the transport, power and communications systems that firms depend on. The GDA's is the best in the State.
points: Dublin Port and Dublin Airport provide the sea and air freight links that move components in and products out.
Motorways radiate from the M50 orbital motorway to the port, the airport and industrial sites, so lorries can reach them quickly.
Reliable, high-capacity electricity and broadband supply suit data-intensive plants.
Rail and bus links bring commuters to business parks and industrial estates, so workers can reach jobs without a car.

notes.b: Government and EU decisions have made Ireland attractive to foreign multinational companies, which choose where to build plants partly on taxes and grants.
points: IDA Ireland, the State agency that attracts foreign investment, promotes the GDA to foreign multinationals and offers sites and grants.
Corporation tax (the tax firms pay on their profits) is 12.5% for most firms.
From 2024, corporation tax rises to 15% for very large multinational groups (turnover over €750 million), under the OECD agreement.
Ireland joined the EEC (the forerunner of the EU) in 1973, giving firms access to European markets.
notes.tip: Quote both tax rates: 12.5% for most firms and 15% for very large multinational groups from 2024.

notes.b: Raw materials are the inputs a factory processes. The GDA has few of its own, so its industries are of two kinds.
points: The GDA has few local raw materials for manufacturing.
High-tech industries import components and ship light, high-value products by air, so distance from raw materials matters little to them.
Food and drink firms process farm produce from the region's hinterland (the surrounding farming area), including the farms of Meath and Kildare.

notes.b: Agglomeration means firms clustering together in one place. Once a cluster starts, it tends to keep growing.
points: Firms cluster together because they can share suppliers, services, skilled workers and transport links.
Once a cluster forms, it attracts further investment and suppliers, which reinforces growth.
Large, concentrated production lowers the cost of each unit produced.

notes.b: The same size and success that attract industry also create costs and risks for firms in the GDA.
points: High costs of land, housing and wages make the GDA expensive for firms.
Traffic congestion delays deliveries and the movement of workers, which raises costs.
A shortage of housing for workers makes recruitment harder.
Manufacturing faces competition from lower-cost countries, because the GDA's wages and land are expensive.
Dependence on multinational firms, which can relocate or cut jobs, leaves the economy exposed.
Global corporation tax changes reduce Ireland's tax advantage, so firms have less reason to choose the GDA.
Strain on electricity and water supply from data centres and growing demand.
notes.tip: For a question asking for one problem or challenge, describe it in detail.

notes.b: Tourism is a tertiary (service) activity. Dublin is Ireland's main gateway for visitors and has many attractions in the city itself.
points: Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are Ireland's main gateway for visitors, so most tourists arrive through them.
The Guinness Storehouse, opened in 2000, is Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction.
The Book of Kells is displayed at Trinity College Dublin.
Croke Park, the headquarters of the GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association), draws visitors to matches and tours, for example.
The Convention Centre Dublin, opened in 2010, supports conference and business tourism (visitors who come for meetings and events).
Good accommodation and transport links support visitors, because tourists need somewhere to stay and ways to get around.

notes.h: Tourism: heritage sites in Meath and Wicklow
notes.b: Beyond the city, ancient and early Christian sites in Meath and Wicklow draw visitors, and a regional brand promotes them together.
points: Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath (Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth), has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place protected as important to all humanity) since 1993.
Newgrange is a passage tomb (a burial chamber reached by a stone passage) about 5,000 years old (about 3200 BC).
Glendalough, a monastic site founded by St Kevin in the 6th century, lies in the Wicklow Mountains National Park.
Powerscourt, Enniskerry, Co. Wicklow, is a historic estate.
Ireland's Ancient East, a Fáilte Ireland brand launched in 2015, promotes the region's heritage.
notes.tip: Tourism questions ask for factors, so name the attractions and say what draws visitors to each.

notes.b: Success brings pressure. Tourism in the GDA faces problems of capacity and competition.
points: Shortages of hotel rooms keep prices high, because demand is greater than supply.
Overcrowding at the most popular sites, such as the Book of Kells, spoils the visitor experience, because crowds make visits slow and uncomfortable.
Traffic congestion in the city centre makes getting between attractions difficult.
The region competes with other European city-break destinations.
notes.tip: Describe tourism challenges without numbers, as there are no checked figures for hotel rates.

notes.b: Transport is both a service industry and an advantage for the region. Dublin's port and airport are the busiest in the State and connect it to Britain and beyond.
points: Dublin Port is Ireland's busiest port, so it is the State's main sea gateway.
Ferries from Dublin Port run to Holyhead, Wales.
Dublin Airport is Ireland's busiest airport, handling over 30 million passengers in 2023.
A north runway opened at Dublin Airport in 2022, adding capacity.
notes.tip: Give only the rounded 2023 figure for Dublin Airport.

notes.b: Within the region, roads and rail link the city to its commuter counties. Most routes radiate from Dublin like the spokes of a wheel.
points: Radial motorways (M1, M3, M4, M7 and M11) run out from the city and are joined by the M50 orbital motorway.
The Dublin Port Tunnel, opened in 2006, takes freight traffic from the port directly onto the motorway network, which keeps lorries off city streets.
DART, the electrified coastal commuter rail line, opened in 1984, so commuters can travel along Dublin Bay without a car.
The Luas tram network, opened in 2004, has Red and Green lines.
Dublin Bus and BusConnects, a redesign of the bus network, provide city and suburban bus services.
MetroLink is a planned rail line from the city centre to Dublin Airport and Swords.
notes.tip: Call MetroLink planned, and give no cost or opening date.

notes.b: Heavy use of transport brings problems, and the authorities have responded with new public transport and a long-term plan.
points: Traffic congestion on radial roads and the M50 slows journeys, because so many commuters use the same routes.
Long commutes from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow into the city add to congestion.
Low-density sprawl makes households car-dependent, because homes are too spread out for frequent public transport.
Responses include investment in public transport, such as DART, Luas and planned MetroLink.
Cycle lanes encourage travel by bicycle, so fewer people need to drive.
The National Transport Authority (NTA) sets out the Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022–2042.
notes.tip: To explain why Dublin has traffic congestion, use commuting from the surrounding counties and car dependence caused by sprawl.

notes.b: Besides tourism and transport, the GDA holds the State's main financial, technology and public services, concentrated in the capital.
points: The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), a district for banking and finance firms, in Custom House Docks, was set up in 1987.
Google's European headquarters, on Barrow Street in Grand Canal Dock, is part of 'Silicon Docks'.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, regenerated the docklands for offices and tech firms.
Government, health and education services are concentrated in the capital, because Dublin is the seat of national government.
notes.tip: Give no staff numbers for Google.

notes.h: Population size and distribution: the figures
notes.b: Census 2022 shows how large the GDA's population is and how it is shared between the counties. The State total was about 5.1 million.
points: Census 2022 counted about 2.1 million people in the GDA, about 40% of the State's population of about 5.1 million.
Co. Dublin had about 1.45 million people; Kildare about 250,000; Meath about 220,000; Wicklow about 156,000.
Dublin city and suburbs had about 1.26 million people; the Dublin City Council area about 590,000.
Co. Dublin has a density of about 1,600 people per km², against a State average of about 73.

notes.b: Population is not spread evenly across the region. Each high-density or low-density area has its own reason, and exam questions ask for those reasons.
points: The highest densities are in Dublin city and suburbs, then in commuter towns along motorways and rail lines.
The lowest densities are on the Wicklow uplands, because steep relief and poor soils limit settlement and farming.
Jobs concentrated in Dublin draw population to the city and its commuter belt.
Lowland relief and fertile soils in Meath and Kildare make settlement and building easier than on the uplands.
Transport routes along motorways and rail lines make commuter towns accessible to Dublin jobs.
notes.tip: A question asking you to account for the distribution of population wants a reason for each high-density and low-density area: relief, soils, jobs and transport.

notes.b: Population dynamics means how a population changes over time. The GDA is growing steadily, and the growth has a pattern.
points: Growth comes mainly from natural increase (births minus deaths): the population is young, with more births than deaths.
In-migration comes from the rest of Ireland and from abroad, because people move for jobs.
The age structure is young and has low dependency (few children and old people compared with working adults) compared with the West.
The population is increasingly multicultural, because immigrants have settled in the region.
Growth is spreading outward into the commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, because people move out to find cheaper housing.
notes.tip: Give no figures for birth rates, average age or migration numbers, as there are no checked figures for the region.

notes.h: Urban development of Dublin: early growth
notes.b: Dublin's growth began over a thousand years ago and was shaped by successive rulers. Georgian Dublin added the planned streets that still define the centre.
points: Dublin was founded as a Viking settlement in 841, which makes it a very old city.
Norman rule expanded the town in medieval times.
The Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and laid out Georgian streets; squares such as Merrion Square were developed by private estates.
Georgian Dublin grew into a planned capital with wide streets and squares.

notes.b: A question on how one urban area developed asks for factors. For Dublin, these are site, route focus, port, capital-city functions, industry and planning.
points: Site: Dublin grew at the lowest bridging point of the Liffey (the lowest place the river could be crossed by a bridge), sheltered by Dublin Bay.
Route focus: roads and routeways radiate from the city, linking it to the rest of the region, so people and goods pass through it.
Port: the harbour on the Liffey gave the settlement a trading role, so the city grew by trade.
Capital-city functions: national government, administration and services concentrate in the city, which creates jobs.
Industry: brewing and food processing grew near the port, because ships brought in materials and carried out products.
Planning: the Wide Streets Commissioners, the Wright Report and the Docklands Development Authority shaped the city's growth.
notes.tip: Organise your answer as factors, each with Dublin-specific detail.

notes.h: Twentieth-century expansion and renewal of Dublin
notes.b: In the 20th century the city spread outward, while its inner areas were rebuilt. Planning and regeneration (renewing run-down areas) drove both changes.
points: Suburban expansion spread the city outward during the 20th century, because more people needed housing.
The Wright Report, 1967, proposed new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin and Lucan.
Ballymun high-rise flats, built in the 1960s, were demolished during regeneration from the 2000s.
Temple Bar was regenerated in the 1990s as a cultural quarter, so a run-down inner-city area gained new uses.
The Docklands and IFSC renewed the inner city, drawing offices and tech firms.
Commuter towns have expanded: Navan and Ashbourne (Meath); Naas, Newbridge and Maynooth (Kildare); Bray and Greystones (Wicklow).

notes.b: Rapid growth has left Dublin with problems that affect both the city and the commuter towns around it.
points: Urban sprawl spreads low-density housing into farmland and commuter towns.
A housing shortage pushes up rents and house prices, because demand is greater than supply.
Homelessness is a serious problem in the city.
Commuting traffic causes congestion on the city's roads, because so many workers travel in at the same time.
Growing demand puts pressure on the water supply.
notes.tip: Keep these problems specific to Dublin and describe them without numbers.

notes.b: In the West, rural areas are losing people. In the counties around Dublin the opposite is true: the countryside is under pressure from the city.
points: Rural areas of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow are under urban pressure, not decline.
Commuter villages grow as city workers move out to live in the countryside, for example in Meath and Kildare.
One-off houses (single houses built in the countryside) and urban-generated housing (housing built for people who work in the city) are built in rural areas.
Rising land prices lead to the loss of farmland to housing.
Growing populations need new schools and services in rural towns and villages, so rural areas are building rather than closing.
Contrast: the West faces rural decline and depopulation.

notes.b: English is the everyday language of the GDA, but Irish and many other languages are also spoken there.
points: English is the dominant language of the GDA, so most daily life is in English.
Nationally, about 1.9 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish in Census 2022; about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.
Gaelscoileanna (Irish-medium schools) are growing in number in the region, so more children are learning through Irish.
Ráth Chairn, Co. Meath, is a Gaeltacht (an area where Irish is the community language) founded in 1935 by families resettled from Connemara by the Land Commission.
Immigration has made the region multilingual; Polish is the most common foreign language spoken at home in Ireland (Census 2022).
notes.tip: Ráth Chairn is a Gaeltacht inside the GDA, so do not say the region has none.

notes.b: The GDA is mostly Roman Catholic, as is Ireland as a whole, but Dublin is less Catholic than the national figure.
points: Nationally, about 69% of people are Roman Catholic and about 14% have no religion (Census 2022).
Dublin has a lower Catholic share and a higher no-religion share than the national figure, so it is more secular than the State as a whole.
The Church of Ireland has a historic presence, shown by Christ Church and St Patrick's cathedrals in Dublin.
Immigration has added Muslim, Orthodox and other communities; the Islamic Cultural Centre of Ireland is in Clonskeagh.
Secularisation (the decline in the role of religion in society) has weakened the role of organised religion in the city.
notes.tip: Give no regional percentage for Dublin, only the national figures.

keyTerms.definition: The core region made up of Dublin City and County Dublin with Counties Meath, Kildare and Wicklow.
The drier lee side of a mountain range, where uplands force moist air to drop its rain on the windward slopes.
A fertile, well-drained soil formed on limestone boulder clay, found in Meath and Kildare.
A deep peat deposit that builds up above the surrounding land in a lake hollow, with a domed surface.
A flat plain of sand and gravel deposited by glacial meltwater, such as the Curragh.
A long, winding ridge of sand and gravel deposited by a meltwater river flowing in or under a glacier.
The intensive growing of field vegetables and glasshouse crops, centred on Fingal.
Horses bred for racing, as in the racehorse industry of Kildare.
A forest of fast-growing evergreen trees, such as Sitka spruce, planted on poor upland soils.
A State-owned port equipped to land and service fishing boats, of which Howth is one.
A power station that pumps water uphill at off-peak times and releases it to generate electricity at peak demand.
The clustering of firms in one area so they share suppliers, services and workers.
A process in which growth in one area attracts further investment and people, reinforcing its advantage.
The spread of low-density housing and development into surrounding farmland and countryside.
A town whose residents travel daily to work in a larger city.
An area where Irish is the community language, such as Ráth Chairn in Co. Meath.
An Irish-medium school, where lessons are taught through Irish.
The decline in the influence of religion on social life and institutions.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area sketch map: what to draw
factCards.definition: The four counties (Dublin and Wicklow on the coast, Meath to the north with a short coastline, Kildare to the west); the Liffey from the Wicklow Mountains to Dublin Bay; the Boyne through Trim and Navan; Dublin, Navan, Naas and Bray; the Wicklow Mountains and the Meath–Kildare lowland.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area climate: why the east is the driest part of Ireland
factCards.definition: Prevailing south-westerlies drop their rain on the Wicklow Mountains and uplands to the west, so the east is in a rain shadow: about 750–1,000 mm a year (Dublin Airport about 750 mm) vs 1,000–1,250 mm in the west. The south-east is Ireland's sunniest part.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area relief: lowland and uplands, with named peaks
factCards.definition: Most of Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin is low, gently undulating lowland of Carboniferous limestone under glacial deposits. The Wicklow and Dublin Mountains have a Leinster granite core; Lugnaquilla (925 m) is Leinster's highest peak; Kippure about 757 m.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area soils: types, locations and land use
factCards.definition: Brown earths on limestone boulder clay in Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin: top farmland. Free-draining sand and gravel on the Curragh: horse training. Raised bog: the Bog of Allen. Acidic podzols and blanket bog (Sally Gap) on Wicklow granite: forestry.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area drainage and Dublin's water supply
factCards.definition: The Liffey rises in the Wicklow Mountains and enters Dublin Bay; its Poulaphouca dam formed the Blessington Lakes (hydro-electricity, drinking water). The Vartry Reservoir at Roundwood also supplies Dublin; Uisce Éireann has proposed a Shannon pipeline.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area agriculture: factors that favour farming
factCards.definition: A dry, relatively sunny climate for tillage and horticulture; flat lowland for large, mechanised fields; deep, fertile brown earths; the huge Dublin market on the doorstep; Dublin Port and Airport for exports; EU and Irish policy and modern technology.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area agriculture: farm types and where they are
factCards.definition: Meath: beef fattening and tillage on large farms. Kildare: bloodstock, with the Curragh racecourse and the Irish National Stud at Tully. Fingal: horticulture (field vegetables, glasshouse crops) around Rush and Lusk. Wicklow: sheep on upland pasture.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area agriculture: problems farmers face
factCards.definition: Urban sprawl takes farmland; high land prices push farmers to sell to developers; part-time farming near the city; costly and scarce seasonal labour for horticulture; competition from imported vegetables; changes to the CAP.

factCards.term: Tara Mines and other mining and quarrying in the Greater Dublin Area
factCards.definition: Tara Mines, Navan: underground zinc and lead mine, opened in 1977, Europe's largest zinc mine, owned by Boliden. Sand and gravel from glacial deposits; granite at Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow. Bord na Móna has ended peat harvesting in the Bog of Allen.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area energy: named sites and facts
factCards.definition: Poolbeg, Ringsend: gas-fired power and the Dublin Waste-to-Energy incinerator (since 2017). Turlough Hill: ESB pumped storage (1974). Arklow Bank: Ireland's first offshore wind farm. Data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing: how its location pattern changed
factCards.definition: Older brewing, food and port industries near Dublin Port and the inner city declined; newer high-tech and pharmaceutical plants are in suburban business parks and towns near the M50 and motorways, such as Grange Castle, Leixlip and Blanchardstown.

factCards.term: Intel, Pfizer and Guinness: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing examples
factCards.definition: Intel, Leixlip, Co. Kildare: opened 1989, Ireland's largest private-sector investment (billions of euro), near the M4. Pfizer: biopharmaceuticals at Grange Castle Business Park, Clondalkin. Guinness: St James's Gate Brewery, founded 1759 on a 9,000-year lease.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing: markets as a factor
factCards.definition: About 2.1 million people, the largest concentration of consumers in the State; Dublin Port and Dublin Airport give access to the EU single market; ferries to Holyhead reach Britain; high-value products are flown out quickly.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing: labour as a factor
factCards.definition: A large, young, educated workforce; graduates from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University; immigrant workers add skills and languages; commuters from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow widen the pool.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing: government policy as a factor
factCards.definition: IDA Ireland promotes the region to multinationals with sites and grants; corporation tax is 12.5%, rising to 15% from 2024 for very large groups (turnover over €750 million) under the OECD agreement; EEC membership since 1973 opened European markets.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area manufacturing: problems and challenges
factCards.definition: High costs of land, housing and wages; traffic congestion; a housing shortage for workers; competition from lower-cost countries; dependence on multinationals that can relocate; global corporation tax changes; strain on electricity and water supply.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area tourism: named attractions with dates
factCards.definition: Guinness Storehouse (2000), Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction; Book of Kells, Trinity College; Convention Centre Dublin (2010); Brú na Bóinne (UNESCO, 1993; Newgrange about 5,000 years old); Glendalough, founded by St Kevin in the 6th century.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area transport: port, airport and roads
factCards.definition: Dublin Port, Ireland's busiest, with ferries to Holyhead; Dublin Airport, Ireland's busiest, over 30 million passengers in 2023, north runway 2022; radial M1, M3, M4, M7 and M11 joined by the M50; the Dublin Port Tunnel (2006).

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area transport: problems and public transport responses
factCards.definition: Congestion on the M50 and radial roads, long commutes from the commuter counties and car dependence from sprawl. Responses: DART (1984), Luas (2004), BusConnects, the planned MetroLink to the airport and Swords, cycle lanes, the NTA's 2022–2042 strategy.

factCards.term: IFSC and Silicon Docks: Dublin's financial and technology services
factCards.definition: The International Financial Services Centre was set up in 1987 at Custom House Docks; the Dublin Docklands Development Authority (1997) regenerated the docklands; Google's European headquarters is on Barrow Street, Grand Canal Dock, in 'Silicon Docks'.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area population: Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: About 2.1 million, about 40% of the State's 5.1 million. Co. Dublin about 1.45 million; Kildare about 250,000; Meath about 220,000; Wicklow about 156,000. Dublin city and suburbs about 1.26 million.

factCards.term: Greater Dublin Area: account for the distribution of population
factCards.definition: Highest densities in Dublin city and suburbs (jobs), about 1,600 people per km² in Co. Dublin against a State average of about 73; then commuter towns along motorways and rail lines; lowest on the Wicklow uplands (steep relief, poor soils).

factCards.term: Dublin's development: site and early growth
factCards.definition: Founded as a Viking settlement in 841 at the lowest bridging point of the Liffey, sheltered by Dublin Bay; Norman rule expanded it; the Wide Streets Commissioners (1757) laid out Georgian streets. Port, route focus and capital functions drove growth.

factCards.term: Dublin's development: 20th-century expansion and renewal
factCards.definition: Wright Report (1967): new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin and Lucan. Ballymun flats (1960s) demolished in regeneration from the 2000s. Temple Bar regenerated in the 1990s; IFSC and Docklands renewal; commuter towns: Navan, Naas, Maynooth, Bray, Greystones.

factCards.term: Language and religion in the Greater Dublin Area
factCards.definition: English-dominant, made multilingual by immigration; growing Gaelscoileanna; the Ráth Chairn Gaeltacht, Co. Meath (1935, Connemara families). Catholic share below the State's 69%; Christ Church and St Patrick's cathedrals; Islamic Cultural Centre, Clonskeagh.

questions.prompt: Account for the development of secondary economic activity in a core Irish region you have studied, with reference to labour and markets.
questions.model: Labour: 1) The GDA has a large, young, educated workforce, which secondary firms need. 2) Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin, Dublin City University, Technological University Dublin and Maynooth University produce graduates for technical and research jobs. 3) Skilled scientists and engineers are available locally, so firms such as Intel at Leixlip can recruit specialist staff. 4) Immigrant workers add skills to the workforce. 5) Commuters from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow widen the pool of workers. 6) A concentration of skilled workers attracts further firms, which share the same labour pool. 7) Intel at Leixlip, opened in 1989, shows how a large firm draws on this skilled labour. Markets: 1) About 2.1 million people live in the GDA, a large home market for manufactured goods. 2) Dublin Port and Dublin Airport give access to the EU single market. 3) Ferries from Dublin Port to Holyhead, Wales, give access to the British market. 4) Dublin Airport allows high-value products to be shipped quickly by air to customers across Europe and beyond. 5) Intel at Leixlip is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, and its high-value products reach world markets by air from Dublin Airport. 6) Pfizer's biopharmaceutical plant at Grange Castle, Clondalkin, is another large secondary firm in the GDA. 7) Ireland joined the EEC in 1973, giving firms access to European markets.

questions.prompt: Examine the factors that have influenced the development of Dublin as an urban area.
questions.model: Site: 1) Dublin grew at the lowest bridging point of the Liffey. 2) The city is sheltered by Dublin Bay. Route focus and port: 3) Roads and routeways radiate from the city, linking it to the rest of the region. 4) The harbour on the Liffey gave the Viking settlement, founded in 841, a trading role. Capital-city functions: 5) National government, administration and services concentrate in the city. Industry and services: 6) Brewing and food processing grew near the port; Guinness's St James's Gate Brewery was founded in 1759. 7) The IFSC, set up in 1987, brought financial services to the Custom House Docks. 8) Google's European headquarters on Barrow Street is part of Silicon Docks. Planning: 9) The Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and laid out Georgian streets. 10) The Wright Report, 1967, proposed new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin and Lucan. 11) Ballymun high-rise flats, built in the 1960s, were demolished during regeneration from the 2000s. 12) Temple Bar was regenerated in the 1990s as a cultural quarter. 13) The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, regenerated the docklands. 14) Commuter towns such as Navan, Naas and Bray have grown with the city's expansion.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one primary economic activity in an Irish region you have studied. (ii) Explain the advantages this region has for this activity. (iii) Describe one problem it faces.
questions.model: (i) Agriculture in the GDA, especially in Meath, Kildare and Fingal. (ii) Climate: the dry, relatively sunny east, in the rain shadow of the Wicklow Mountains, suits tillage and horticulture. Relief: flat lowland allows large fields and mechanised farming. Soils: deep, fertile brown earths of Meath and Kildare, among the best farmland in Ireland. Market: about 2.1 million people in the GDA, and Dublin Port and Dublin Airport for export of farm produce and livestock. (iii) Problem: urban sprawl takes farmland for housing, and high land prices push farmers to sell land to developers, especially near Dublin.
